                                        PROJECT NO. 58482

    LARGE LOAD DEMAND                               §            PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
    MANAGEMENT SERVICE                              §                          OF TEXAS
                                                    §


The stated purpose of Senate Bill 6 and filing 58482 is to establish a regulatory framework to
manage the rapid growth of Large Loads. Demand management is the most effective way to
control the impact of these large loads without stifling the economic growth they provide across
Texas. Senate Bill 6 currently prohibits LLDMS resources from dual-participating in another
reliability service, ancillary service, ERS, wholesale-price demand response, or a TDSP DR
program, which forecloses the dual-participation model described in the next section under the
rules proposed in 58482. Voltus includes the cross-jurisdictional example from PJM nonetheless
because it reflects better market design by allowing dual participation in complementary
services, and offers a model the Commission may wish to revisit as LLDMS matures or in a
future rulemaking.

Cross-Jurisdictional Example: Dual Participation in PJM
Several other jurisdictions allow dual participation across different services in order to maximize
the value that each participating load provides. In PJM, resources can be simultaneously enrolled
in capacity, energy, and ancillary services programs. Rules around program hierarchy govern
simultaneous dispatch and payment to ensure that no single megawatt is getting paid for two
different services during the same hour. For example, a load that participates in Economic
Demand Response1 may choose to curtail in response to PJM’s 5 Coincident Peak (5CP)2 peak
hours. During this hour, the site may not claim earnings in Economic Demand Response for their
curtailment.

Similarly, when Emergency Load Response Program (ELRP)3 dispatches coincide with PJM’s
5CP hours, PJM adds back curtailed MW to customer Peak Load Contribution (PLC)
calculations. These add-backs ensure that performance counts for ELRP only. The process is as
follows:



1
  In PJM, Economic Demand Response refers to electricity consumers voluntarily reducing their energy
consumption in response to high wholesale electricity prices.
2
  5CP are the five individual single-hour periods across the entire summer season when electricity demand
across the PJM region reaches its highest levels.
3
  ELRP is PJM's main Demand Response (DR) initiative. It allows large electricity consumers
(commercial, industrial, and institutional end-users) to earn payments by voluntarily reducing their power
usage when the electric grid is under severe stress or approaching capacity limits.
    ●​ PJM identifies the system peak (5CP) hours that determine generation capacity charges,
      and load’s Peak Load Contribution (PLC) during those hours.
   ●​ If ELRP dispatch coincides with the 5CP hours, PJM "adds back" the curtailed
      megawatts to the load’s PLC.
   ●​ The load’s PLC for next year gets reconstituted for peak shaving instead of reflecting the
      lower usage during peaks. This eliminates capacity savings from peak avoidance because
      the site gets no credit for reducing load during peaks.

To prevent payments for different services in the same hour, PJM has a clear hierarchy of which
programs get paid for energy during overlapping dispatches:
   1.​ ELRP
   2.​ 5 Coincident peak (5CP)
   3.​ Economic Demand Response

Voltus recommends that, to the extent not precluded by legislation, the PUCT develop an
analogous hierarchy and system of add-backs to allow dual-participation between LLDMS and
4CP.

Current Regulatory Dependencies in ERCOT
It is nearly impossible to evaluate the exclusions the PUCT has laid out in §25.521 section (c)(2)
while filing 58000, NPRR 1337, and Batch Zero are all under consideration.

Filing 58000 Dependencies
If implemented, filing 58000 could transition ERCOT’s coincident peak methodology for
transmission cost recovery to 12 monthly peaks (12CP) rather than the 4 monthly peaks (4CP)
that exist today. The CP framework in general risks undercharging highly flexible loads, or loads
with substantial onsite resources, in that total peak avoidance does not imply zero reliance on the
transmission system or zero contribution transmission cost causation; the proposed changes
under 58000 are designed to mitigate this risk. The proposed 12CP design makes it harder for
loads to avoid transmission charges: just because a large load has historically been responsive to
coincident peaks under the 4CP framework does not mean they will be able and willing to curtail
in response to all 12 monthly peaks under 12CP. Further, ERCOT achieves its goal of reducing a
large load’s ability to avoid all transmission costs by introducing the minimum demand charge
laid out in 58000. If transmission cost recovery is structured such that Large Loads cannot
avoid paying their fair share, Voltus would like to ensure that loads responding to
coincident peaks can also participate in LLDMS.

NPRR 1337 Dependencies
NPRR 1337 proposes significant changes to ERS which, if realized, will drastically reduce ERS
procurement by restricting price-responsive resources. As such, pricing will increase in ERS,
 meaning that ERS and LLDMS will be competing for the same non-price-responsive load
resources. These two programs should serve different load classes to maximize available
flexibility across different load management products.

ERS and LLDMS as written today serve nearly the same purpose on the transmission system: to
provide load shed during an emergency. If given the choice between ERS and LLDMS, these
large loads will almost certainly choose ERS because it provides a more stable source of revenue
than that associated with energy-only payments in emergency conditions under LLDMS. From
the initial rules laid out by the PUCT, it is unclear what each large load’s minimum obligated
volume must be to LLDMS (aside from the minimum bid of 1 MW). If 1337 is approved, new
non-price-responsive loads will enter ERS, and LLDMS procurement will remain low.

The value that price-responsive loads provide during an emergency is incremental to the volume
already being economically curtailed. Allowing this dynamic makes sense: if the price signal
alone is not achieving the necessary level of response to meet emergency conditions, then
ERCOT needs another tool to preserve reliability. By implementing a meter-before-meter-after
baseline for price-responsive resources, ERCOT will be able to accurately quantify this
incremental value without excluding these loads entirely. Exclusion of price-responsive
resources makes sense in ERS because resources are paid for availability, whereas in LLDMS
the same resource is paid for curtailment only. Voltus recommends keeping LLDMS open to
price-responsive loads in order to maximize participation from resources leaving the ERS
market.

Batch Zero Dependencies
Under the Batch Zero process, it is unclear whether loads operating as provisional controllable
load resources (PCLRs) would qualify for LLDMS. Loads registered as PCLRs are allowed to
interconnect only after ERCOT has established their firm Low Power Consumption (LPC) limit
and Maximum Power Consumption (MPC) limit. PCLRs can consume between LPC and MPC
but must accept dispatch obligations to curtail above their LPC. PCLRs must comply with SCED
Base Point instructions and are subject to dynamic bid capping, meaning that they contain a
non-firm portion of load that is visible, controllable, and responsive to ERCOT.

As of now, the Batch Zero process is paused. ​On August 3, 2026, Governor Greg Abbott sent a
letter directing the PUCT and ERCOT to conduct a comprehensive audit of all data center
projects in the ERCOT interconnection queue. Once this audit has been completed, PCLRs will
begin the interconnection process again. The PFP set forth in 58482 must establish whether
these loads are immediately eligible for LLDMS, or will only become eligible after their
established PCLR exit date.
 Responses to PUCT Questions
   1.​ Proposed subsection (f)(1)(C) authorizes payment to a qualified scheduling entity
       representing a large load customer that is not instructed by ERCOT to deploy but is
       subject to availability verification during the Large Load Demand Management Service
       (LLDMS) obligation period. Should a large load customer that is available but not
       ultimately instructed to deploy during the LLDMS obligation period be compensated
       some percentage of the market clearing price for the large load customer' s availability to
       reduce demand during the LLDMS obligation period? If so, what is an appropriate
       payment to the large load customer for their availability during the LLDMS obligation
       period?

       In short, yes. ERCOT will benefit by paying rents for availability to deliver. Successful
       emergency load response programs across other jurisdictions use a payment structure that
       includes both energy and capacity payments. While capacity payments are set during the
       auction cycle, energy payments are earned during emergency dispatch. Voltus
       recommends this same structure to create incentives for Large Load participation even if
       an emergency seems unlikely.

       For example, PJM ELRP is a capacity program where performance is calculated for
       each Performance Assessment Interval (PAI) as the difference between a site’s seasonal
       static baseline and its actual load. Static baseline is set to the load’s Peak Load
       Contribution (PLC), which is ​determined by averaging a facility's electricity demand
       during the previous year’s 5 Coincident Peaks. During an emergency dispatch, the site
       earns energy payments on a $/MWh basis at the real-time locational marginal price
       (LMP). A similar structure would incentivize both availability and curtailment in
       LLDMS, without overpaying participants for a contract term where no emergency event
       occurred.

   2.​ Proposed subsection (f)(4) imposes a maximum budget of $54 million in a calendar year.
       What is an appropriate budget for the LLDMS program?

       Voltus concurs with the comments submitted by Potomac Economics which stated that a
       fixed seasonal or annual budget does not fit the sporadic nature of extreme weather
       events. A year or season in which no event occurs (whether due to mild weather or
       simply a low risk of firm load shed) should not have the same budget as a year/season
       with an event like Winter Storm Uri occurs.

   3.​ What cadence should ERCOT use to assess an extreme weather condition and how far in
       advance should ERCOT start the auction to procure LLDMS?
    ERCOT should assess the probability of firm load shed and, if sufficiently high, should
   dispatch the LLDMS whether or not an extreme weather event is present. ERCOT should
   procure LLDMS on regular intervals (biannually, seasonally, or monthly) instead of only
   on an as-needed basis to ensure sufficient resources are available when events occur.
   Procuring LLDMS only shortly before an expected extreme weather event gives too
   much leverage to the participating loads: by even holding an auction, ERCOT is
   signalling that an emergency event has been forecasted. Participants will be incentivized
   to drive up the clearing price. Regular procurement neutralizes this signal and will
   incentivize participants to bid in at their true cost of curtailment.

4.​ Should ERCOT be allowed to deploy LLDMS for transmission emergencies? If so, what
    limitations, if any, should the Commission impose on this authority?
    Yes, ERCOT should be permitted to deploy LLDMS for transmission emergencies, not
    only for system-wide capacity or energy shortfalls. The same compensation structure
    should apply here as for other LLDMS emergency deployments. Localized transmission
    constraints can occur even when total system capacity is otherwise adequate, and large
    loads sited near a constrained facility can materially affect the severity and duration of
    those events. Limiting LLDMS to capacity emergencies alone would leave the
    Commission without a tool to manage a significant share of the reliability risk that large
    loads create.

   At the same time, ERCOT should not assume that every transmission emergency must be
   solved by managing the large load itself. Distributed capacity assets located at the large
   load’s site, or elsewhere on the distribution system, can offset a load’s impact on the
   transmission system as effectively as the large load’s own curtailment, and in some cases
   without requiring the load to reduce its operations at all. The Commission should
   evaluate a large load’s contribution to a transmission emergency by measuring the net
   effect on the constrained transmission assets provided by other loads managed on its
   behalf, not solely by the MW volume curtailed at the large load itself. The product should
   treat distribution-level effects as part of the transmission solution rather than something
   outside LLDMS’s scope.

   Voltus proposes that the Commission build a bring-your-own supply (BYO) framework
   into LLDMS. This should include crediting distribution-level effects toward
   transmission-emergency relief. Because BYO assets typically interconnect at the
   distribution level, their contribution to relieving a transmission emergency should be
   measured and credited at the point where the constraint occurs, not discounted because
   the asset sits below the transmission system. ERCOT’s authority to deploy LLDMS for
   transmission emergencies should explicitly recognize distribution-connected capacity and
   demand response as legitimate, and often faster, alternatives to transmission-level
 intervention alone. Note that a BYO framework would also provide relief during supply
shortfalls unrelated to transmission constraints.

On limitations, Voltus recommends that any transmission-emergency deployment of
LLDMS be limited to net new contribution: a large load that is already self-flexing, or
already reducing its net demand through onsite or distribution-connected resources,
should not be compensated to provide the same service twice. What LLDMS
compensates should be capacity or curtailment that is additional to what the load is
already providing the system.
